items.prompt: Try it first. You are White and it is the very first move. Play a pawn move that takes space in the centre. Not sure? Press a hint.
hints: The centre is the middle four squares: d4, e4, d5 and e5.
Two of White's pawns can reach the centre on the first move.
Move the pawn in front of the king, or the one in front of the queen, two squares.
items.explain: Either pawn frees a bishop and the queen: e4 opens the bishop on f1 and the queen on d1 along their diagonals, and d4 opens the bishop on c1 and the queen on d1. The engine rates both as top choices.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white knight on c4 can move to. Count them as you tap.
hints: A knight jumps in an L: two squares one way, one square the other.
Count the jumps up, down, left and right of c4. Nothing blocks a knight.
There are eight squares: a3, a5, b2, b6, d2, d6, e3, e5.
items.explain: This knight is two files in from the edge, so none of its eight squares is off the board. A knight on the b-file would lose two of its eight squares. The corner and the edge are the poor squares.

items.prompt: Black to move. White's queen and bishop both aim at f7. Find a move that stops a quick checkmate.
hints: Which Black pawn is the target, and how many White pieces aim at it?
You can attack the queen, or add a guard to the pawn.
Several moves hold: a pawn move that attacks the queen, or a move that adds a guard to f7.
items.explain: The pawn on f7 is guarded only by the king, and two White pieces aim at it. Pushing the g-pawn attacks the queen and is the sharpest answer [V depth 16]. Qe7, Nh6 and Qf6 also add a guard and hold. The natural developing move Nf6 loses at once, because it does not deal with the threat.

items.prompt: White to move. White's knight on f3 is out. Bring a bishop to a square where it does something.
hints: Which bishop has an open diagonal now?
The e-pawn moved, so the bishop on f1 is free.
Look for a diagonal that points at Black's pieces.
items.explain: The bishop on f1 has been free since the e-pawn moved. Both squares put it on an open diagonal aimed at Black's side. The engine rates both as top choices.

items.prompt: White has brought both knights out, but not the bishop. Can White castle kingside right now? Predict, then check.
hints: Castling needs the squares between the king and the rook to be empty.
Which square between e1 and h1 is still occupied?
Look at f1.
items.explain: The bishop is still on f1, between the king and the rook, so castling is not allowed. Moving the bishop first is the usual fix.

items.prompt: Black to move. White has just taken a pawn on d5. Taking it back with the knight is natural. Is that recapture safe? Predict, then check.
hints: Count which White pieces aim at f7 once the knight on f6 has left.
The knight on g5 and the bishop on c4 both look at the same square.
Compare with a move that does not leave f7 to the king alone.
items.explain: The recapture Nxd5 moves the knight away and leaves f7 guarded only by the king, with two White pieces aiming at it. The knight jump to f7 then forks queen and rook. A quiet retreat such as Na5 hits the bishop first and is the engine's choice [V depth 16].

items.prompt: Black to move. White has just played a quiet pawn move. Is the developing move Bc5 a good choice here? Predict, then check.
hints: Does White threaten anything against Black right now?
Black has two natural developing moves for the bishop; check whether this is one of them.
The bishop move aims along a diagonal toward f2.
items.explain: Nothing is threatened, so developing is the right kind of move. The engine puts Bc5 and Be7 within a few hundredths of a pawn of each other [V depth 16].

items.prompt: Black to move. This time White's last move was the knight jump to g5. Is the developing move Bc5 still a good choice? Predict, then check.
hints: Has White's last move created a threat?
Count the White pieces aiming at f7.
Compare this with the position where White played a quiet pawn move instead.
items.explain: White's last move added a second attacker on f7, so there is a threat to answer. The same developing move that was fine one move earlier now costs about a pawn.

items.prompt: White's bishop has already moved twice (to b5, then a4). Is a third bishop move, Bb3, a mistake because of that? Predict, then check.
hints: Black's pawn move attacked the bishop. What are the bishop's choices?
Compare the retreat with capturing the knight or leaving the bishop in place.
Is 'each piece once' a law, or a habit with conditions?
items.explain: The bishop was attacked, so it has to move, and the retreat keeps it on its diagonal. The habit says do not waste time; here no time is wasted. The engine's top choice is the retreat.

items.prompt: White to move, early in the game and nothing is threatened. Play a useful move, and say to yourself which habit it follows.
hints: Is anything threatened? If not, which pieces are still at home?
The king is already safe. What helps the centre or the last pieces?
A pawn that supports the centre, a rook to the middle, or the last knight all work.
items.explain: Nothing is threatened and White has already castled, so the habits point at finishing development and supporting the centre. The engine rates a4, c3, Re1, Bb3, Nc3 and Nbd2 within a few hundredths of a pawn [V depth 16]. When several moves are equal, choose by plan.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white bishop on c1 can move to. A pawn has moved, so some squares are open.
hints: The bishop moves diagonally.
The d-pawn has left, so one diagonal is open.
Five squares on the diagonal running to h6.
items.explain: The d-pawn moved two squares, so the diagonal from c1 to h6 is open. The bishop on c1 now reaches five squares, where before it reached none.

items.prompt: You are Black and White has played the king pawn two squares. Take a share of the centre with a pawn, or bring a piece toward it.
hints: The centre is d4, e4, d5 and e5. Which of your pawns can reach it or watch it?
Two pawns claim the centre; two others fight for it from the side.
Move the pawn in front of the king, a pawn on the c-file, or a knight toward the middle.
items.explain: Black can meet the centre pawn with e5 to take its own space, fight for the centre from the side with c5, e6 or c6, or develop the knight to c6. The engine rates all five within a few hundredths of a pawn [V depth 16]. The d5 push is also played, but the engine rates it about a third of a pawn lower [V].

items.prompt: White has moved the bishop and the squares between king and rook are empty. Can White castle kingside right now? Predict, then check.
hints: Castling needs empty squares between the king and the rook, but it has one more condition.
The king crosses f1 on its way to g1.
Is f1 attacked by a Black piece?
items.explain: The squares are empty, but the king would pass over f1, and the Black bishop on a6 attacks it along the long diagonal. A king may not castle out of, through or into check.

items.prompt: White to move. Black has used two moves on one knight. Use the spare time: bring out another piece or castle.
hints: Count the pieces each side has brought out.
White is a move ahead in development. How can that move be used?
Castle, develop the last knight, or hit the knight with a pawn.
items.explain: Black spent two moves on one knight, so White is a move ahead in development. Castling, the knight to c3 and the pawn to c3 all use that time [V depth 16]. [I] Much of White's edge here comes from the lost tempo, though the knight on b4 is also loose.

items.prompt: White to move. Bring out a knight to the square that is clear whatever Black does next.
hints: Knights jump, so they are never blocked by pawns.
Each knight has a natural square toward the centre.
The knight on g1 and the knight on b1 each have one.
items.explain: A knight's good squares do not depend on the pawns, so it can come out at once. The bishop's best square depends on what Black's pawns do. Nf3 is the engine's first choice and Nc3 is close behind [V depth 16].

items.prompt: You are Black and White has opened with a knight. Take a share of the centre or bring out a piece toward it.
hints: White did not play a centre pawn. What can you play in the centre?
A pawn to d5, a knight to f6, or a pawn that supports the centre all follow your habits.
Choose a move that takes space or develops.
items.explain: Against a knight opening Black has several good ways to follow the habits: the d-pawn, a developing knight, a supporting pawn, or the c-pawn. The engine rates all four within a few hundredths of a pawn [V depth 16].
